complete_source_units.text: After the Sabbath they gave a share of the spoils to the maltreated, the widows and the orphans, and divided the rest among themselves and their children.

Yet he did not cease his haughtiness at all, but was still filled with arrogance, breathing fire in his anger against the Jews and ordering the journey hastened. He happened to fall from the chariot as it rushed along, and in the severe fall all the members of his body were wrenched.
No one could carry the man who a little earlier thought he could touch the stars of heaven, because of the unbearable weight of his smell.
The defiled man made vows to the Master who would no longer have mercy on him, speaking in this way:
Besides these things, he would become a Jew and go through every inhabited place, proclaiming God’s might.
As the fifth day dawned, twenty young men of Maccabeus’s company, burning with anger because of the blasphemies, attacked the wall courageously and cut down whoever they met with a beast-like fury.
Maccabeus himself was the first to take up his weapons. He urged the others to share the danger with him and help their brothers. Together and eagerly they set out.
Together they all blessed the merciful God and grew strong in spirit, ready to pierce not only human beings but the fiercest wild animals and iron walls.
Rushing like lions upon the enemy, they struck down eleven thousand of them and sixteen hundred horsemen; they forced all the rest to flee.

The people of Joppa committed this great impiety. They invited the Jews living among them to board boats that they had provided, with their wives and children, as though there were no hostility toward them,
The nations in Judea who had driven Judas into exile joined Nicanor in crowds, thinking the Jews’ misfortunes and disasters would become their own successes.
He urged him to marry and have children. Judas married, settled down and shared in ordinary life.
A certain Razis, one of Jerusalem’s elders, was reported to Nicanor: a man who loved his fellow citizens, was very well spoken of, and because of his goodwill was called a father of the Jews.
The thrice-accursed man asked whether there was a Sovereign in heaven who had commanded the observance of the Sabbath day.
Arming each of them with the encouragement of good words more than with the security of shields and lances, he also related a trustworthy dream, a kind of waking vision, and gladdened them all.
